title: SAT vs ACT: How Do You Make the Best Choice for You?
summary: Compare the ACT and SAT side by side: timing, sections, math, science and scoring. Take a free full-length practice test of each (no credit card required).
body_markdown:
The digital SAT and the enhanced ACT are both accepted by colleges; choosing one depends on your strengths and how you prefer to test. Below we compare format, content, and scores so you can decide.


## ACT vs SAT: key differences at a glance


The following table highlights the structural differences between the digital SAT and the enhanced ACT:


Feature Digital SAT Enhanced ACT


Total Test Time 2 hrs 14 min 2 hrs 5 min (plus 40 minutes per optional section: Science and/or Writing)


Total Questions 98 questions 131 questions (Core sections)


Pacing More time per question Less time per question


Format Digital and adaptive Paper or digital, linear


Score Range 400–1600 1–36


## SAT and ACT content and structure compared


The feel of the content differs significantly between the two tests:


### SAT vs ACT reading and writing


-


**SAT:** Features very short, single-paragraph passages with one question each. Text and vocabulary tend to be more complex.


-


**ACT:** Uses longer passages accompanied by multiple questions per passage. Vocabulary is generally more direct and school-style.


### SAT vs ACT math: What's different?


-


**SAT:** Focuses deeply on Algebra, Geometry, and Trigonometry with a focus on problem-solving. About 25% of the section requires student-produced responses.


-


**ACT:** Covers a broader variety of topics, including more Geometry and Trigonometry. Questions are generally more straightforward but fast-paced.


### Science: SAT vs ACT


-


**SAT:** There is no standalone Science section; data interpretation is integrated into the Reading, Writing, and Math sections.


-


**ACT:** The Science section is now optional and its score is reported separately from the Composite score.


### Calculator use: SAT vs ACT


-


**SAT:** Desmos, a built-in graphing calculator, is available for the entire Math section. Students may also use an approved personal graphing calculator.


-


**ACT:** Desmos is also available for the entire digital Math section. Students may also use an approved personal graphing calculator for both paper and digital formats.


Desmos is available on both the digital SAT and the ACT math section. To get the most out of it, see our[Desmos cheat sheet for the SAT](https://acely.com/sat-prep/desmos-cheat-sheet) . For more on the SAT's structure and pacing, read our[complete SAT prep guide](https://acely.com/sat-prep/ultimate-sat-2026-guide) .


## Practice and preparation: Try both tests


For free full-length SAT practice tests and lessons, take a[Bluebook](https://bluebook.collegeboard.org/) test and then review and learn concepts in[Khan Academy](https://www.khanacademy.org/digital-sat) . However, this won't help you compare to the ACT. The best way to decide which test fits you is to take one full-length practice of each with a platform like[Acely](https://acely.com/sign-up) , and compare your scores.


You can then create a personalized study plan for both the SAT and ACT if you decide to take an official test in both and see how you perform on test day. For more SAT and ACT resources, see our[SAT prep hub](https://acely.com/sat-prep) .


### Cost and registration


Both tests have similar base registration fees (around $68). The ACT charges extra for the optional Writing section and, in some cases, the optional Science section. Check the[College Board](https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/registration) and[ACT](https://www.act.org/content/act/en/products-and-services/the-act/registration.html) websites for current fees and test dates.


## ACT vs SAT: which test should you choose?


Most colleges accept both tests, so you should decide based on your personal strengths:


-


**Choose the SAT if:**


- You prefer a more deliberate pace with more time to think through each question.
- You excel at evidence-based reasoning and analyzing short, dense texts.
- You are comfortable with an adaptive format that adjusts difficulty as you go.


-


**Choose the ACT if:**


- You are a naturally fast test-taker who can handle less time per question.
- You prefer a linear test where the difficulty does not change.
- You want the option to choose between a digital or a traditional paper-and-pencil exam.
- You want to take a Science section (if you're applying to a STEM program for example).


To make the best decision, take a full-length practice test for both on a platform like[Acely](https://acely.com/sign-up) to see which format feels more natural for you.


### How to decide between the SAT and ACT


Most colleges accept both the SAT and ACT, so your choice should match your strengths and format preferences. Here's how to decide:


1. Compare format and timing using the key differences table above.
2. Read the "Choose the SAT if" and "Choose the ACT if" lists to see which aligns with your strengths.
3. Take one full-length practice test for each (e.g. on[Acely](https://acely.com/sign-up) ).
4. Compare your scores and how the tests felt; focus prep on the test that fits you better.

For middle 50% score ranges by college, use the school lookup on the[ACT to SAT conversion](https://acely.com/where-to-start/act-sat-conversion-chart#school-score-requirements) page.


## FAQs


Admissions offices treat both tests equally. The official concordance tables from the[College Board](https://research.collegeboard.org/reports/data-tables-technical-resources/concordance) and[ACT](https://www.act.org/content/act/en/products-and-services/the-act/scores/act-sat-concordance.html) allow you to find comparable scores between the two exams. An ACT composite of 30, for example, maps to an SAT total of roughly 1360–1380. Use our[ACT to SAT conversion](https://acely.com/where-to-start/act-sat-conversion-chart#conversion-table) chart for a full side-by-side comparison of test scores across both exams.


Most high school students begin SAT prep during the spring of their sophomore year or the summer before junior year. Starting early gives you enough time to build skills, take practice tests, and prepare for potential retakes.


Most high school students begin their test prep in the spring of their sophomore year to allow time for potential retakes and also minimize stress in junior and senior year. By starting in the sophomore year, students can have more time in junior year to prepare for AP exams and start college applications before the fall of their senior year.
